must_remember: The Zeeman effect is the splitting of spectral lines in the presence of a uniform magnetic field.
The Normal Zeeman effect is observed in singlet states ($S = 0$) where a line splits into exactly 3 components ($\Delta m = 0, \pm 1$).
The Anomalous Zeeman effect occurs when $S \neq 0$, resulting in more than three components, requiring the Lande $g$-factor.
Landé $g$-factor is expressed as $g = 1 + \frac{J(J+1) + S(S+1) - L(L+1)}{2J(J+1)}$.
Selection rules for Zeeman transitions are $\Delta m_j = 0, \pm 1$.
The Stark effect is the splitting of spectral lines by an electric field, whereas the Zeeman effect is caused by a magnetic field.

glossary.meaning: Splitting of a singlet spectral line into three components when placed in a magnetic field.
Splitting of spectral lines into more than three components for systems with non-zero total spin.
A dimensionless factor accounting for the unequal contributions of orbital and spin angular momenta to the magnetic moment.
Fundamental unit of magnetic moment for an electron, $\mu_B = \frac{e\hbar}{2m}$.
Frequency of precession of a magnetic moment about an external magnetic field, $\omega_L = \frac{eB}{2m}$.
